metadata.title: BI Dashboard Extensions Platform Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how a Hardenberg and London based extensions vendor with about 30 employees, 30+ extensions, 600+ customer organisations in 150+ countries and 32 partners would need to change when the platform it lives inside ships native equivalents of its products, tightens the Extensions API and safelisting rules, or loses a large customer to Power BI; when a US bank's vendor assessment fails and North American procurement asks for different evidence and terms; when a customer disputes the anonymous-token user count behind its invoice; when the Tableau Visionary co-founder leaves after the Vortex buyout; when AI generates bespoke dashboards for free; when a top partner builds a competitor; when a self-hosted upgrade breaks hundreds of workbooks; or when the group acquires an add-on company with a different runtime.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: An organisation subscribes on the website, in the Tableau Exchange or through a partner, and picks Free, Professional or Enterprise. Dashboard creators drop SuperTables, ShowMeMore, PowerKPIs and DashboardGuide into Tableau dashboards; the extension web apps load from Infotopics' SaaS hosting or, for Enterprise customers, from a self-hosted ExtensionsManager installation that needs no internet. Every extension calls the license service, which meters anonymous unique user tokens over a rolling twelve months and produces the annual invoice. WriteBackExtreme and InputTables write forecasts, comments and corrections into the customer's own databases with an audit trail; MailScheduler renders dashboards to PDF, PNG, CSV and Excel and delivers them to email, Teams, Slack and network drives; partners resell and implement in their region; questions arrive in the support portal and docs.infotopics.com. The design assumes that Tableau keeps loading extensions the way it does today, that a feature sold as an extension stays absent from the platform, that a customer stays on one BI platform for the life of the contract, that one security story and one contract serve every country, that a token is a user, that the founders stay, that a partner stays a partner, that an extension URL never changes, and that the company has one runtime and one licence service.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design separates extension, feature and platform-native equivalent; organisation, entitlement, plan and platform; extension manifest version, Extensions API version, host URL, hosting mode, safelisting record and workbook binding; platform adapter and platform-neutral configuration, write-back schema, schedule and saved view; legal entity, currency, contract template, hosting region, product release, dependency inventory, security finding, evidence document and incident; counting rule version, token, usage event, reconciliation mode, usage report and dispute; role, person, platform relationship and architectural decision record; AI task, generated artifact, governed dataset, human decision and data-residency policy; partner tier, agreement version, registered deal, end-customer ownership and pipeline share; and legal entity, runtime, licence model mapping and account and identity federation for acquired products. An organisation can change BI platform, hosting mode, extension version, partner or reseller, and the vendor can lose a feature to the platform, add a region, a currency, a certification or an acquired runtime, without the customer losing its licence, its write-back data, its audit trail, its schedules or its dashboards.
metadata.note: The stressors start in the Tableau ecosystem the company was born in: the 2018 Extensions API, Exchange safelisting, Salesforce's native roadmap, the Power BI and Looker Studio ports since 2022, the anonymous-token metering model, the 32-partner channel, and the Vortex thesis of AI functionality plus selective acquisitions. They are not forecasts and assign no likelihood; each asks what must remain after the vendor is pushed into a different attractor. The Extensions API change and the failed bank assessment are recorded as residues the company already carries; the self-hosted upgrade scenario is the loop that tests whether those residues hold without new structure.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: Salesforce ships native Viz Extensions, write-back and Pulse that absorb the value of SuperTables and ShowMeMore
stressors.detection: Tableau release notes and Dreamforce and Tableau Conference keynotes, the Viz Extensions and Tableau Pulse roadmap, Tableau Exchange listing policy changes, native table, input and write-back betas, Power BI matrix and Copilot updates, free-plan signups for SuperTables and ShowMeMore flattening, renewal conversations that cite 'included in Tableau', partner win-loss notes, and feature requests shifting to what the native product still lacks.
stressors.attractor: The platform vendor makes the most-used extension native and free. Customers who bought SuperTables for pivoting, grouping and Excel export, or ShowMeMore for chart types the platform lacked, now see a good-enough version inside Tableau at no extra licence, and ask why they pay per active user for the rest. The naive design sells features extension by extension; when a feature becomes native, that extension's price collapses, and a 30-person company cannot out-build Salesforce feature by feature.
stressors.businessReaction: Move the value from single features to workflows the platform vendor will not build: governed write-back into the customer's own databases, planning and approvals, distribution to people who are not Tableau users, guidance and usage evidence, and Excel-grade grids on millions of rows. Reposition the portfolio as a per-organisation decision layer priced by active users rather than a shopping list of extensions, retire or make free any extension the platform absorbs, measure which extension features are still used after each Tableau release, and carry the same products to Power BI and Looker Studio so absorption on one platform does not end the business.
stressors.residue: Separate extension, feature, platform-native equivalent and its version, entitlement per organisation and plan, price line and bundled portfolio. Value and price attach to workflows and to the organisation's active users, not to a feature the platform can replicate; an extension can be retired, made free or folded into a bundle without changing the customer's licence.

impacts.effect: Creators keep a reason to build with the extensions after the platform copies the obvious features: governed workflows, not chart types.
Delivering an Excel-friendly dashboard relies on grid depth, saved views and write-back rather than on features Tableau now ships natively.
The renewal case is built on workflow usage per active user, with absorbed features shown as retired rather than as lost value.
Monthly active dashboard users is measured per workflow and platform so native absorption of one feature is visible without hiding total adoption.
The creator-side business outcome tracks bundle and workflow revenue per organisation instead of revenue per extension.
Concentrates on server-side row model, saved views, formulas and Excel-grade interaction that a native table does not offer, and drops features the platform absorbs.
Becomes a bundled storytelling layer whose chart types can be retired one by one as Viz Extensions arrive.
Sells a plan for the organisation's decision workflows rather than a list of extensions.
Guides creators from native building blocks to extension workflows where the platform stops.
Keeps a feature registry with native-equivalent status per platform version and telemetry on which features are still used.
Is structured as a chart library where each chart type carries a retirement path once Tableau ships it natively.
Prices plans per organisation and active users with bundled entitlements, so an extension can be made free without touching the invoice.
Reports which extension features carry adoption after each platform release to support retire-or-invest decisions.
Owns the retirement and bundling decisions with tables and discovery and deployment and licensing.
Owns grid depth beyond native tables and the feature registry with the extension runtime team.
The creator checks the native feature first and reaches for an extension only where it still adds governed write-back, Excel-grade tables or delivery the platform lacks.
Native Viz Extensions, Pulse and subscriptions set the floor that every premium extension must clearly exceed.

stressors.name: Tableau tightens the Extensions API, sandboxing and safelisting rules and hosted extensions stop loading
stressors.detection: Tableau Extensions API changelog, deprecation and sandboxed-extension policies, content security policy and iframe changes in Tableau Cloud releases, Exchange listing requirements, Tableau Server safelist behaviour per version, extension framework error rates per Tableau version, support tickets that spike on the day a Tableau Cloud release rolls out, and Power BI custom visual certification changes.
stressors.attractor: A Tableau Cloud release changes how extensions are loaded, what a sandboxed extension may call, or which domains an administrator may safelist. Overnight, hundreds of organisations open dashboards whose SuperTables and PowerKPIs show an empty frame. The naive design binds the extension's code, its host URL, its Extensions API version and its stored settings into one bundle, so a platform change breaks all of them at once and the vendor learns about it from customers.
stressors.businessReaction: Run a pre-release test matrix against Tableau beta and pre-release channels, version the extension framework against Extensions API versions with feature detection and graceful fallback, keep a canary set of customer-like workbooks per Tableau version, publish compatibility status per extension and platform, make host URL, manifest version and settings schema independent so a workbook can be repointed without rebuild, keep the self-hosted runtime as the escape when SaaS hosting is restricted, and maintain the relationship with the Tableau product team as a formal alliance rather than a personal one.
stressors.residue: Separate extension manifest version, Extensions API version, host URL, hosting mode (SaaS or self-hosted), sandbox policy, safelisting record, workbook binding, settings schema version and compatibility status. A dashboard's binding to an extension is a versioned reference that can be repointed, and the runtime detects what the host platform allows and degrades feature by feature rather than failing whole.

impacts.effect: Platform leads run extensions that survive a Tableau release without a Monday-morning outage.
Governing which extensions run includes a compatibility status per extension, Tableau version and hosting mode.
Keeping every workbook on the right extension version and URL becomes a bulk binding change rather than workbook edits.
Extension upgrade lead time includes the time to repoint bindings after a platform change.
Monthly active dashboard users is protected against release-day gaps by graceful degradation.
Positions the self-hosted runtime as the safelisted, platform-change-resistant option for regulated customers.
Makes TrexReplacer the bulk repointing tool for manifest version and host URL changes.
Carries safelisting record, manifest version and compatibility status through install and upgrade.
Shows creators the compatibility status of each extension for the Tableau version they publish to.
Detects the host's Extensions API version and sandbox policy and degrades features instead of failing.
Isolates data fetch, filter and parameter sync behind an API-version adapter with a tested fallback.
Runs the pre-release test matrix, canary workbooks and per-extension compatibility publication.
Records host URL, manifest version and safelist state per deployment and repoints workbooks in bulk.
Owns API-version adaptation and the release test matrix with deployment and licensing.
Owns hosting modes, safelisting metadata and the compatibility status feed.
Safelisting becomes a versioned policy per platform release, with a sandboxed fallback build approved alongside the hosted one.
Rival extension studios face the same API change; the vendor with a certified sandbox-mode build wins the re-approval cycle.

stressors.name: A large customer moves from Tableau to Power BI mid-contract and expects the same extensions on the new platform
stressors.detection: Enterprise-wide BI consolidation announcements, Microsoft 365 and Fabric bundling, Tableau renewal quotes, customer questions about Power BI or Looker Studio parity, active-user tokens falling on the Tableau side while AppSource installs rise, partner reports of migration projects, and CIO surveys on BI standardisation.
stressors.attractor: A named enterprise with a thousand Tableau users standardises on Power BI because it comes with Microsoft 365. Its Enterprise licence for WriteBackExtreme, SuperTables and MailScheduler has eighteen months to run, its planners rely on write-back forms and its executives on scheduled reports. The naive design licenses per Tableau deployment: entitlements, workbook bindings, write-back schemas and schedules are Tableau-shaped, so the customer either loses the workflow or the vendor loses the customer.
stressors.businessReaction: License per organisation across platforms so the entitlement travels with the customer, keep write-back schema, audit trail, saved views and schedules in platform-neutral stores, provide migration tooling that maps Tableau workbooks and extension configurations to Power BI visuals and Looker Studio community visualizations, publish a parity matrix per product and platform, price the migration at zero within the running contract, and use the migration to sell the decision layer to the customer's Power BI centre of excellence.
stressors.residue: Separate organisation, entitlement, platform, platform adapter, extension configuration (platform-neutral core plus platform binding), write-back schema, schedule, saved view and parity status per feature. A customer can change BI platform without changing licence, data, audit trail or workflow, and a feature can exist on one platform before another.

impacts.effect: Platform leads keep the extensions investment when the organisation changes BI platform.
Planners keep entering forecasts in the same write-back schema and audit trail after the dashboard moves to Power BI.
Renewal evidence covers active users across Tableau, Power BI and Looker Studio under one entitlement.
Planning cycle time is held constant through a platform migration because the write-back workflow does not restart.
The platform-lead business outcome tracks retained subscription value per organisation across platform changes.
Becomes the landing place for migrating customers with a published parity matrix and migration tooling.
Keeps its data store, roles and audit trail platform-neutral so a Tableau write-back app becomes a Power BI one.
Runs the same workflow on any supported platform against the same customer database.
Counts active users per organisation across platforms and moves the entitlement with the customer.
Carries the platform-neutral extension configuration into Power BI visuals and Looker Studio visualizations with feature parity status.
Separates the configuration core from the platform binding so settings survive a platform change.
Keeps write-back schemas, records and connectors independent of the dashboard platform.
Expresses one entitlement per organisation across Tableau, Power BI and Looker Studio.
Renders and schedules reports from Power BI and Looker Studio sources as well as Tableau.
Owns platform-neutral configuration and adapters with every extension team.
Owns write-back portability with the extension runtime team.
Runs migration cohorts with a named customer success manager per migrating organisation.
The planner keeps the same grid, validation rules and audit trail after the move because InputTables and WriteBackExtreme run on the multi-platform adapter.
A Power BI native planning visual is the default replacement offered by the migration partner unless parity exists on day one.

stressors.name: A US bank's vendor assessment fails on a hosted-extension finding and North American procurement demands SOC 2, USD terms and a breach clause
stressors.detection: Vendor-risk questionnaires (SIG, CAIQ), requests for SOC 2 Type II next to ISO 27001, penetration-test findings on hosted extension endpoints, dependency vulnerability advisories in the extension bundles, data-flow questions about what a SaaS-hosted extension sees, sub-processor lists, US procurement asking for W-9, USD invoicing, indemnity and breach-notification clauses, deal cycle time by country, and cyber-insurance conditions.
stressors.attractor: A US bank's third-party risk team finds that a SaaS-hosted extension's JavaScript can read every mark in the dashboard and calls a licence endpoint in the Netherlands, then asks for a SOC 2 report the company does not have, USD pricing and a contract under New York law. A finding in one extension bundle is treated as a finding against the whole vendor. The naive design ships one security story (ISO 27001, annual penetration test, on-premises option) and one contract for every country, and a 30-person company answering each questionnaire by hand cannot close enterprise deals in its largest market.
stressors.businessReaction: Publish a trust centre with per-product data-flow documentation, sub-processors and what the hosted extension can and cannot see; add a software bill of materials and dependency scanning per release; run the SOC 2 Type II examination alongside ISO 27001; offer a US hosting region and the self-hosted runtime as the default answer for regulated customers; create a US legal entity with a USD price list and US-style contract templates; treat security incidents per product and release with a customer notification workflow; and equip partners to carry the assessment in their region.
stressors.residue: Separate legal entity, currency and price list, contract template and governing law, hosting region, product, release, dependency inventory, security finding, evidence document (ISO, SOC 2, penetration test, data flow), sub-processor, incident and notification. Security evidence is a versioned catalogue per product and release and commercial terms are per entity and region, so one finding, one country or one contract form no longer blocks the whole business.

impacts.effect: Security reviewers get evidence per product and release in the format their regulator and procurement expect.
Assessing the vendor starts from a trust centre with data flows, SOC 2 and ISO evidence and a bill of materials per product.
Safelisting decisions are backed by per-extension data-flow documentation and hosting region.
Vendor assessment cycle time is measured per country and evidence set, not as a single average.
The security-side business outcome tracks enterprise deals closed in regulated sectors and regions.
Adds a US hosting region, self-hosted default for regulated customers and per-release security evidence.
Gives regional partners the assessment kit and contract templates for their market.
Produces evidence per product, release and region and routes incidents to affected organisations.
Quotes in the buyer's currency and contract form from the entity that serves its region.
Maintains the versioned evidence catalogue, dependency inventory, findings, incidents and notifications per product and release.
Hosts per region with a software bill of materials and dependency scanning in the release pipeline.
Invoices from the right legal entity, currency and contract template.
Documents identity data flows and offers customer-managed SSO as assessment evidence.
Carries regional assessment kits, contract templates and deal protection to partners.
Owns the evidence catalogue and incident process with deployment and licensing and the extension runtime team.
Owns hosting regions, entities, currencies and contract templates.
Owns the North American go-to-market with partners carrying regional assessments.
The evidence pack ships as a trust-centre bundle with SOC 2 type report, ISO 27001 certificate, pen-test summary and per-deployment data-flow diagrams on request.
A competing on-premises write-back vendor with US procurement paperwork ready becomes the fallback shortlisted by the bank.

stressors.name: A customer disputes the active-user count behind its invoice and asks how anonymous tokens are generated, stored and audited
stressors.detection: Renewal invoices that exceed the plan's user band, token counts that jump after a Tableau Server upgrade or browser policy change, customer requests for the token list, procurement asking how a user is counted when tokens follow browsers and devices, disputes escalated through partners, data-protection questions on whether an anonymous token is personal data, and differences between DashboardUsage numbers and license-service numbers.
stressors.attractor: A Professional customer near 100 users receives an Enterprise-tier invoice because a browser reset created new tokens for the same people and a Tableau Server upgrade started counting embedded-dashboard visitors it never saw before. The customer asks for evidence and the vendor has a counter, not a ledger. The naive design stores a rolling count per organisation; it cannot show which tokens, on which dashboards, on which days, through which extension, and cannot reconcile against the customer's own Tableau user list without turning anonymous tokens into personal data.
stressors.businessReaction: Make the token record explainable: per token, first seen, last seen, extension, dashboard host, hosting mode and counting-rule version, with a customer-visible usage report in the Enterprise Customer Portal that DashboardUsage agrees with; publish counting rules with effective dates and grace bands; offer reconciliation modes (token, Tableau site user through the customer's own identity provider, or named user) chosen by the customer; give account managers and partners a dispute workflow with credit notes; and keep tokens pseudonymous by design with a documented data-protection assessment.
stressors.residue: Separate organisation, plan, counting-rule version, token, usage event, dashboard host, reconciliation mode, usage report, invoice line, dispute and credit. Metering becomes an auditable ledger with a rule version rather than a counter, and the customer sees the same numbers the invoice is built from.

impacts.effect: Platform leads can explain and challenge the user count their subscription is priced on.
Renewal justification uses the same usage ledger the invoice is built from.
Licence governance includes choosing the reconciliation mode and reviewing the counting rule in force.
The platform-lead business outcome is tracked net of disputed and credited usage.
Partner-side business outcomes distinguish partner-resolved disputes from lost renewals.
Adds the customer-visible usage report, counting rules with effective dates and the dispute workflow to the Enterprise Customer Portal.
Aligns DashboardUsage with the license ledger so adoption and billing numbers agree.
Carries counting-rule version, reconciliation mode, dispute and credit through metering and invoicing.
Feeds adoption evidence from the same usage events the license service counts.
Stores tokens and usage events as a ledger under a versioned counting rule and produces invoice lines from it.
Shows the usage report, counting rule and dispute status to the customer.
Reads the same usage events as the license service so both reports reconcile.
Enables the site-user and named-user reconciliation modes through the customer's identity provider.
Owns the metering ledger and counting rules with distribution and adoption and support and enablement.
Aligns DashboardUsage with the metering ledger.
Runs the dispute workflow with account managers and partners.
The platform lead sees the same rolling 12-month token count the invoice uses, with an exportable audit of how tokens map to sites and workbooks.
Portal vendors that price per named user become the comparison point in the dispute.

stressors.name: The Tableau Visionary co-founder leaves after the buyout and the platform relationship, product judgement and ecosystem standing leave with him
stressors.detection: Earn-out and lock-up terms, founder role changes in the post-buyout plan, conference speaking slots and Tableau Visionary renewals, community activity and blog cadence, roadmap decisions that used to be one person's call, key-engineer retention, recruiting velocity in Hardenberg and London, and customer and partner questions about who leads product.
stressors.attractor: The CTO who built the first extension in 2018, sits among the 25 global Tableau Hall of Fame Visionaries and knows the Tableau product team personally leaves within two years of the buyout. Early access to betas, keynote demos, Exchange relationships and the intuition for what Tableau will build next were personal, not institutional. The naive organisation depends on a founder as the interface to the platform, the architect of the runtime and the face of the company to 32 partners.
stressors.businessReaction: Institutionalise the platform relationship with named alliance owners per platform, a written compatibility and roadmap-watch process and several community voices rather than one; document the extension framework, release pipeline and architectural decisions; establish a product council across the four extension teams; use the Vortex thesis to hire a product leader and a platform alliances lead; put retention agreements on the critical few; and make partner relationships owned by a team, not a person.
stressors.residue: Separate role, person, platform relationship, community standing, architectural decision record, product decision forum and retention agreement. Knowledge of the platform and of the runtime lives in documented decisions, processes and teams, and a person can leave without the company losing its access to the platform or its judgement about it.

impacts.effect: Partners keep a company-level relationship and roadmap access when a founder steps back.
Enablement and partner margin come from a programme owned by a team rather than from founder relationships.
Governance decisions rely on published compatibility and roadmap-watch outputs rather than on a founder's early knowledge.
Partner-sourced subscription revenue is tracked per partner owner so a leadership change shows up per relationship.
Dashboard requests delivered per month keeps its trend through a product leadership change because roadmap decisions have a forum.
Assigns each partner a named owner and moves enablement content into the programme.
Follows a product council roadmap rather than one person's sense of what Tableau will ship.
Runs on documented partner ownership, deal registration and enablement calendars.
Keeps creator guidance grounded in a maintained compatibility and roadmap-watch process.
Carries architectural decision records and documented framework contracts so the runtime is not one person's knowledge.
Documents the release pipeline and platform-listing processes as runbooks.
Records partner owner, relationship history and programme commitments per partner.
Hosts the architectural decision records, roadmap-watch notes and community content from several voices.
Owns the decision records and platform alliance process with the product council.
Owns team-level partner and platform relationships.
Contributes community presence and product judgement through the product council.
Roadmap intake moves from founder conversations to a partner advisory board with a published quarterly plan.
Consultancy-born rivals recruit the same Tableau community talent that the departure loosens.

stressors.name: AI generates a bespoke dashboard in a minute, so the case for one interactive dashboard with extensions has to be remade
stressors.detection: Tableau Agent and Pulse, Copilot in Power BI and Gemini in Looker generating visualisations from prompts, LLM-generated workbooks and SQL, dashboard requests per month falling because business users generate their own views, free-plan signups shifting to AI-native tools, customer questions about AI in the extensions, accuracy incidents where generated dashboards show the wrong number, and governance teams banning ungoverned AI dashboards.
stressors.attractor: The core sales argument was that one SuperTables dashboard replaces ten bespoke dashboards. If a business user can ask an agent for a bespoke view in a minute, the scarcity that justified the extension disappears. At the same time AI-generated dashboards multiply ungoverned numbers, and planners still cannot write a forecast back through a chat. The naive product treats AI as a feature inside each extension (generative fill) and has no place for AI as a competitor to the dashboard itself.
stressors.businessReaction: Move the argument from fewer dashboards to governed decisions: the extensions become the governed surface where AI drafts a table, an explanation or a plan and a human writes back the decision with an audit trail; ship AI-assisted configuration so a creator builds an extension-based dashboard as fast as an agent generates a bespoke one; expose extension data and write-back as tools an agent can call under the organisation's roles; measure whether AI-generated views replace or feed the governed dashboards; and keep the customer's data in the customer's environment for every AI call.
stressors.residue: Separate AI task, prompt context, model and provider version, generated artifact, governed dataset, human decision, write-back commitment, audit record and data-residency policy. AI proposes and explains inside the customer's environment, and nothing it proposes becomes a plan number, a report or a configuration without a recorded human action.

impacts.effect: Viewers get AI answers inside a governed dashboard rather than another ungoverned bespoke view.
Answering my own question includes an AI draft over the governed dataset, with the numbers still traceable.
Comments, corrections and approvals can start from an AI-drafted explanation but are committed only by a person.
Self-service answer rate counts AI-assisted answers inside the governed dashboard separately from ungoverned generated views.
Dashboard requests delivered per month is complemented by AI-assisted configuration time so the creator argument holds against generated dashboards.
Adds AI drafting of tables, groupings and explanations over the governed data with generative fill kept auditable.
Becomes the human-decision surface where AI-drafted plans are reviewed, corrected and committed with audit trail.
Includes AI draft, governed dataset and traceable answer as explicit steps.
Adds AI-proposed values with approval and audit as distinct records.
Runs AI tasks with context, model version, generated artifact, residency policy and audit as first-class records.
Exposes grid data and configuration as agent-callable tools under the organisation's roles.
Records the human decision and approval on every AI-proposed write-back.
Provides the governed dataset and lineage that AI drafts and explanations are bound to.
Owns supervised AI patterns with tables and discovery, write-back and planning and the extension runtime team.
Owns AI drafting inside the grid and the agent-callable interface.
Owns human approval of AI-proposed plan values.
Generative fill and AI explanations live inside the governed table, so the viewer gets AI speed without leaving the certified dashboard.
Copilot-generated reports in Power BI make instant bespoke dashboards the baseline the extensions must beat on governance and depth.

stressors.name: A top partner builds or resells a competing write-back extension and takes its clients with it
stressors.detection: Partner job postings for extension developers, a partner's own Tableau Exchange listing, deal-registration volume by partner falling while its client list grows, partners requesting source access or white-label terms, platform partner tiers rewarding native adoption, margin renegotiation, joint customers receiving a competing proposal, and partner-sourced revenue concentration by firm.
stressors.attractor: A global consultancy with thousands of Tableau consultants decides governed write-back is a product it can own, builds or acquires one, and stops recommending WriteBackExtreme in the accounts it controls. Because partner relationships, demo licences, deal registration and joint delivery are informal and the largest partners bring a disproportionate share of Enterprise deals, the naive design loses pipeline, references and market knowledge on the day the partner changes sides, and has no direct relationship with the end customer.
stressors.businessReaction: Make the direct customer relationship primary: every Enterprise licence has a named customer success manager and portal account regardless of who sold it; formalise the partner programme with tiers, deal protection, margin per tier and a no-compete window for enablement material; diversify across the 32 partners and regions so no firm exceeds a set share of pipeline; publish extension APIs so partners extend rather than replace; and treat the departing partner's clients as a migration cohort with a retention offer.
stressors.residue: Separate partner, partner tier, agreement version, registered deal, end-customer account, customer success ownership, demo entitlement, margin schedule, pipeline share and competitor status. A partner can change from reseller to competitor without the vendor losing the customer, and pipeline concentration is a monitored quantity rather than a surprise.

impacts.effect: Partners work inside a programme with clear tiers, protection and margin, and know where extending ends and competing begins.
Winning and delivering extension projects runs on registered deals with protection and published APIs for partner add-ons.
Recurring margin follows a tiered schedule with enablement terms rather than a handshake.
Partner-sourced subscription revenue is tracked with concentration per firm and region.
The partner-side business outcome monitors pipeline share per partner against a concentration limit.
Adds tiers, deal protection, margin schedules, agreement versions and competitor status.
Publishes APIs and extension points so partners build on it instead of replacing it.
Carries registered deal, tier and end-customer ownership from onboarding to renewal.
Assigns a named customer success manager to every Enterprise organisation regardless of channel.
Records partner tier, agreement version, registered deals, pipeline share and competitor status.
Owns the direct relationship and the retention cohort when a partner departs.
Gives every end customer its own account and portal independent of the reseller.
Exposes REST and extension points under partner licence terms.
Owns the formal programme and concentration monitoring with support and enablement.
Owns direct customer success ownership for partner-sold organisations.
Deal registration carries exclusivity windows and margin tiers that reward partners for staying on the vendor's write-back stack.
A partner-built or resold planning suite is the most likely replacement offer a departing partner brings to shared clients.

stressors.name: An on-premises upgrade of the self-hosted extensions changes the extension URL and breaks hundreds of workbooks at once
stressors.detection: ExtensionsManager upgrade logs, extension URL and port changes after a server move or certificate renewal, Tableau Server safelist entries that no longer match, workbook counts per extension URL, tickets that arrive as 'all dashboards are grey' on a Monday morning, TrexReplacer usage spikes, and differences between the customer's staging and production Tableau versions.
stressors.attractor: An IT administrator upgrades the self-hosted runtime, moves it to a new host or renews a certificate; every workbook still points at the old URL, the safelist entry no longer matches, and a thousand-user deployment sees blank extensions until each workbook is edited by hand. The naive deployment treats extension URL, version and safelist as facts inside each workbook.
stressors.businessReaction: Keep the residues from the Extensions API stressor and the vendor-assessment stressor in place: versioned workbook bindings that TrexReplacer repoints in bulk, tenant deployment records that know host, version, URL and safelist state, release evidence per version and a staged upgrade path; add an upgrade rehearsal and compatibility report in ExtensionsManager before switching production, and a rollback to the previous binding.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: the separation of workbook binding, manifest version and host URL from the Extensions API residue, and the per-release, per-deployment evidence from the security residue, already express the repointing, the compatibility check and the rollback. The scenario confirms that a self-hosted upgrade is a binding change, not a workbook change.

impacts.effect: IT administrators upgrade, move or re-certify the runtime without touching a single workbook.
Installing and upgrading without downtime reuses the staged upgrade path and rollback binding.
Keeping workbooks on the right version and URL is one bulk repoint with a compatibility report.
Extension upgrade lead time holds for host moves and certificate renewals as well as version upgrades.
The IT-side business outcome counts upgrade-caused outages per deployment against the rehearsal step.
Composes upgrade rehearsal, compatibility report and rollback from existing deployment records.
Uses TrexReplacer as the bulk repointing step of every upgrade.
Includes rehearsal, repoint and rollback as steps built on existing bindings.
Repoints bindings in bulk, rehearses upgrades and rolls back from the deployment record.
Reads the versioned binding rather than a hard-coded URL in the workbook.
Shows the customer which release and binding each deployment runs and what the rehearsal reported.
Routes upgrade incidents to the deployment record instead of to individual workbook tickets.
Owns the upgrade path with the extension runtime team and support and enablement.
Prepares administrators through documentation and rehearsal guidance.
The upgrade runbook pins extension URLs behind a stable alias and rehearses TrexReplacer on a workbook sample before the window opens.
Report-distribution vendors with fully hosted delivery point at self-hosted upgrade pain in competitive deals.

stressors.name: Vortex adds an acquired add-on company with its own runtime, licence model and customers to the portfolio
stressors.detection: Vortex buy-and-build moves, term sheets for Tableau or Power BI add-on vendors, overlap between the target's products and the 30+ extensions, the target's runtime (a different framework, hosting or licence server), customer and partner overlap, security and compliance due-diligence findings, and integration staffing for a company of about 30 people.
stressors.attractor: The buyout thesis promises selective acquisitions; the first target ships Power BI visuals on its own framework, licenses per named user through its own portal, hosts in a different cloud and has customers who also use a competitor of SuperTables. Rewriting the target onto the extension framework would consume the runtime team for a year; leaving it separate gives customers two portals, two licences, two security stories and two support desks. The naive design assumes one runtime, one licence service and one portal.
stressors.businessReaction: Federate first: one customer account and identity across portals, one entitlement model that can express the target's licence as a plan, one trust centre with the target's evidence as a separate catalogue, and one support entry point; then decide per product whether it becomes native on the extension framework, stays on its own runtime behind the adapters, or is retired; keep the target selling to its own customers; and set integration milestones the small teams can carry.
stressors.residue: Separate legal entity, product line, runtime, licence model mapping, customer account federation, identity federation, evidence catalogue, support routing and capability ownership. An acquired product is a federated partner with shared account, entitlement and trust, and a roadmap to become native only where it pays.
